value.overview: The Ochraceous Pewee (Contopus ochraceus) is a small, distinctive tyrant flycatcher of the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is associated mainly with montane forest edges, clearings, and open areas near high-elevation woodland. The species is usually recognized by its warm ochraceous-brown plumage, relatively long wings, upright posture, and habit of making short sallies from exposed perches to catch flying insects.
value.classification: The Ochraceous Pewee belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Contopus, which includes several pewees and related aerial insectivores. It is treated as a distinct species, Contopus ochraceus.
value.identification: This is a small to medium-sized pewee with generally warm brown or ochraceous upperparts and paler underparts washed with buff or cinnamon tones. The wings are darker, with subtle pale edging or wing bars, and the bill is broad at the base, as in many flycatchers. It often sits upright on an exposed twig, fence, or dead branch. Its repeated short flights from a perch to seize insects are useful for identification.
value.rangeHabitat: The Ochraceous Pewee has a restricted Central American range, occurring in the highlands of Costa Rica and extending into western Panama. In Costa Rica it is principally a montane and high-elevation species, where it may be found along forest borders, shrubby clearings, open woodland, roadsides, and other semi-open habitats near humid mountain forests. It generally favors cool upland environments and can occur in disturbed landscapes when suitable perches and nearby insect-rich vegetation remain available.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally considered resident or largely sedentary within its mountain range. In Costa Rica, individuals normally remain in highland regions year-round, although local movements may occur with elevation, weather, food availability, or seasonal habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited compared with that of better-studied widespread flycatchers. Like related Contopus species, it is expected to form breeding territories in suitable montane habitat and to nest during the local wet-season period when insect prey is abundant. The nest is likely placed on or near a branch or other elevated support, but detailed information on nest sites, clutch size, incubation, and parental care is not well documented in widely available sources.
value.dietFeeding: The Ochraceous Pewee feeds mainly on flying insects and other arthropods. It commonly uses a visible perch and makes quick aerial sallies to capture prey, then returns to the same or a nearby perch. This sit-and-wait strategy is typical of pewees and is especially effective along forest edges, clearings, and open mountain vegetation where insects pass through the air.
value.behavior: This species is usually encountered alone or in pairs and often appears calm while perched upright and scanning for prey. Its short, direct flights from exposed perches are characteristic. It may defend a feeding or breeding territory with calls and aerial activity, but it is not generally known for large flocks or conspicuous long-distance movements. Dense cover, mist, and high-elevation conditions can make it difficult to detect despite its use of open perches.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not confidently quantified in widely available summaries. The species has a restricted highland distribution, so local habitat changes may be important even though it is not currently classified as globally threatened.
